drivers.story: Oliver Shah drives in from the southern estate on Thursdays to induct new starters; on his other office day, he can usually join by video. He reads the road notices in the paper over breakfast and gives himself eight minutes to find a free space rather than pay for the office car park.

Bethan Walker does accounts from her kitchen on the southern estate and normally asks clients to scan their receipts. One shopkeeper still saves his in a biscuit tin, so she collects it on the same trip as her weekly shop, after the lunchtime television bulletin and before the school traffic.

Fiona Morgan drives her diesel from the southern estate to unlock the bakery before the first bus runs. When the borough posts a diversion, she pins the map in the bakers' group and sets her alarm earlier; the night baker has a bus of his own to catch.

Peter Singh keeps the village hall accounts from home and drives his little diesel down the valley for the monthly cash count, when two people have to sign. He clips the hall notices from the local paper and pencils the bus times beside them for meetings that finish before the last service.

Daniel Patel can review drawings from his flat on the southern estate, but on Tuesdays he drives in to lay the full-size plans out with the site team. He has the television on while he packs lunch, though it's the parking tariff he checks before leaving: the early rate ends at eight.

Jane Kaur walks from her market-town flat to the office except when it's her turn to bring the display boards to a client meeting. She follows the signed delivery route she saw demonstrated on local television and books the loading bay for a quarter of an hour, long enough to carry everything upstairs.

Harriet MacLeod drives out of the market town for the early laundry shift, collecting a press operator who puts cash towards the long commute. A vague traffic item on breakfast television bothers her less than an empty doorstep at pickup time: they have ten minutes to spare between them.

Imran Morgan threads his small diesel through the outer ring on his breakfast care round; at the third house he helps a man dress before his day-centre ride arrives. He reads the neighbourhood group for street closures but keeps his own notebook of which entrances save five minutes with a walking frame.

William Evans does accounts at home in the valley villages, but most Saturdays he makes the long drive to collect his daughter for the weekend. Conflicting posts about the bridge leave him uneasy, so he asks her what the approach looks like from her bus stop before they agree a pickup time.

Gareth Green drives from the southern estate to a packing depot on the far side of town, where his paid hours start when he clocks in. When the television traffic report and the shift chat disagree, he rings the gatehouse; he hates losing a quarter-hour's pay on the strength of a forwarded picture.

Bethan Taylor works on payroll from her outer-ring bungalow and drives across town to rehearse with a choir, a journey she can skip when the monthly returns are due. She keeps the concert listing from the paper beside her mileage book; with parking on top of petrol, a second rehearsal in the same week takes some budgeting.

Kiran Singh leaves the market town before dawn in his small petrol car to relieve the night porter at a conference centre. He takes a photo of the paper's roadworks map to share in the porters' chat, but times the drive himself before promising his colleague an early getaway.

Aisha Taylor drives the short stretch from the market town to the cold store because her shift finishes well after the buses stop. A clip from the television news keeps turning up in her shift chat without its date, and she worries about sending the childminder a pickup time she can't keep.

Peter Morgan does accounts at home on the southern estate and picks up his uncle for the bowling club's afternoon session. He checks the fixture in the paper rather than setting off when the first club message arrives; his uncle likes ten quiet minutes to change his shoes.

Daniel Reed's home-care round starts on the northern estate and takes his roomy petrol car across town twice before lunch. He keeps numbered mileage slips behind the visor because a missed claim comes out of his grocery money, and checks road closures mentioned in the carers' chat against the council notice.

Aisha Wilson drives a roomy petrol car from the southern estate to the bottling plant, with three colleagues taking the other seats on late shift. They split the parking charge, and when the supervisor posts a gate change she moves their pickup time ten minutes earlier without much fuss.

Leanne Wilson drives from the southern estate to the hospital laundry and has to collect her son from breakfast club on the way home after nights. She reads the local paper on her break, but when the parents' chat starts guessing about opening hours she calls the club; its late fee is more than she earns in half an hour.

Ruth Walker starts her care round in the market town and covers enough outlying houses to fill a page of her mileage book each day. She marks the roadworks from the weekly paper on her folding map; the visit she plans around is lunch with a client who needs the full half-hour to eat.

Alison Begum drives a long way from the northern estate on the two days she staffs the office reception desk; she does the booking sheets at home the rest of the week. She listens closely to the breakfast television travel bulletin because the colleague waiting to hand over has a train to catch.

Nina Jones drives from the northern estate to a distribution shed two towns away for twelve-hour shifts. She watches the weather map on television with her boots already on, trying to judge how much sleep she can afford before the next early start on that long road.

Bethan Morgan's first care call on the southern estate is a two-person lift, so a second worker is waiting at the door at seven. She trusts the local television road bulletin and notes any extra driving time on her rota rather than cutting minutes from the visit.

Alison Wilson drives her diesel from the market town to the dairy for the evening testing shift, a short run but too late for a bus home. She pays more attention to the gate attendant's messages in the shift group than to the television traffic map; six minutes at the wrong entrance can mean missing the first batch.

Sophie Iqbal drives a diesel estate from the valley villages for office presentations but chairs the follow-up meetings from home. She saves official diversion maps from the council feed alongside her parking receipts; an unexpected extra hour on the road means paying her dog walker for a second call.

Imran Owen drives from his valley village to the next one to take over the evening shift at a supported-living house. Photos of water on the ford turn up in his group chat without a time stamp, so he asks the outgoing worker which way she came; the bridge adds ten minutes.

Since retiring, Fiona Hughes has driven boxes of large-print books from the outer ring to a lunch club twice a month, though a club member can collect them if she packs them the night before. She circles changes of venue in her paper and rings the organiser to be sure; a wasted round trip makes a noticeable dent in her pension.

Eleanor Wilson works at her kitchen table in the market town except on client days, when she drives across the valley with a case of sample folders. A delay on the breakfast news bothers her enough to check the town group for a time and place; she has ten minutes to spare before the client arrives.

Imran Lewis keeps accounts from his flat on the outer ring and rarely takes his small diesel out except to collect a client's box of receipts. He reads the parking notices in the paper, but checks the sign himself before putting coins in the meter; the handover takes barely three minutes.

Jane Campbell makes a short circuit of the outer ring, dropping her son at school and then helping her father into his coat for the day-centre minibus. She hears the traffic report on television while packing lunch, but it's the four minutes her father needs for those last few buttons that she builds into the drive.

Nina Evans drives from the market town to open a bakery before the first bus runs; arriving three minutes late leaves the flour delivery sitting on the pavement. She watches the late television bulletin before bed and takes the signed diversion without fuss when one is announced.

Oliver Kaur lives near the suburban station, but no train gets him to the sorting depot for the night handover. He checks the shift group's posts for photos of the depot entrance before setting off; circling round to the other gate costs six minutes and keeps his partner on the loading bay.

Eleanor Jones takes her mother along on the short school run around the outer ring so they can go straight on to her podiatry appointment. She hears the local news on television but rings reception for practical details, especially whether the five-minute drop-off gives her time to unfold the walker.

Since retiring, Farah Jones has driven boxes of library books from the outer ring to a lunch club, where she has three minutes at the side door before the meal van needs the space. She trusts the librarian's posts about access, but leaves the neighbours' busy discussion thread unread and packs the boxes in unloading order.

Harriet MacLeod usually works from her northern estate home, but on induction days she takes the diesel car in with two monitors for a new starter. She watches the television travel report while the kettle boils and allows eight extra minutes for the posted diversion rather than trying a side street.

Callum MacLeod lives in the rail suburb and joins most meetings from home, but his regular branch visits put plenty of miles on his little petrol car. He takes television estimates of journey times with a pinch of salt and copies the branch manager's habit of booking a visitor space; it saves ten minutes of hunting with a laptop bag on the passenger seat.

Bethan Davies barely moves her diesel car most weeks: her desk is at home and the office in the next valley village only needs her for the occasional signing. The television bulletin's advice to allow six minutes at the bridge goes straight onto her calendar; she hates the thought of keeping a witness waiting.

Oliver Wilson collects his daughter from school on the southern estate and drives her straight to her speech appointment, with six minutes between the bell and the latest they can leave the gate. Conflicting pickup times in the parents' group make his stomach knot, so he checks the slip in her schoolbag himself.

Sophie Shah's little petrol car covers a long loop from the northern estate to two schools and her brother's house, where she takes over care of their aunt. She listens to the television news and keeps the paper's roadworks map in the glovebox; six minutes lost at the first school can leave her brother paying for a taxi to work.

Callum Green does payroll from the southern estate, but likes the long drive to play chess with his old club; on deadline evenings he can play online instead. A travel warning on television makes him uneasy even when the details sound vague, and he generally goes along with his teammates if they suggest saving the car-park fee.

Eleanor Fraser drives her diesel from the rail suburb on a round of home-care visits, starting with a man who needs help getting from bed to his breakfast chair. The rota gives her just three minutes between two nearby doors, so when a colleague posts about a broken entry buzzer she calls ahead rather than leaving the next client waiting.

Jane Reed's small petrol car stays parked in the market town most days, since she can walk to the office or work at home. She drives when it's her turn to return the archive crates, catching the headlines on television before she leaves; the free five-minute loading space matters more to her than a quicker route to a paid bay.

Sophie Kaur drives out from the southern estate for an early laundry shift and has to be changed before the first linen cages arrive. She follows the local television report and pencils the paper's published roadwork dates onto her rota, worried that the six minutes she normally has for changing won't stretch to a detour.

Oliver Allen drives from the northern estate to relieve the attendant at a cold store; the man coming off shift has a bus to catch eight minutes later. Oliver worries about that connection, but after seeing different closure times on television and in his social feed he phones the gatehouse rather than passing either time on.

Aisha Kaur works from a valley village and drives a long way to the main office when a trainee needs her beside the desk rather than on a screen. She takes the television travel bulletin seriously, but works out her own departure time: the visitor gate admits cars for just three minutes before the delivery lorries get their turn.

Thomas Reed works partly from home and usually walks across the market town to his desk, driving only when it's his turn to bring back the office projector. He doesn't put much stock in traffic forecasts on television; he follows the caretaker's advice to use the yard, where four minutes of unloading costs nothing.

Leanne Iqbal drives in from the northern estate to take minutes at the monthly board meeting; for routine office days she can log in from home. A television item about new parking charges has her checking the small print in the paper, since the board reimburses her mileage but not the cost of a bay.

Fiona Jones does accounts from her market-town home, but her roomy petrol car gets plenty of use carrying her keyboard to rehearsals around the valley. Parking eats into the band's takings, so when television coverage and the musicians' social feed disagree about evening charges she asks the venue to quote the price before agreeing to drive.

Callum Kaur is retired and takes a neighbour from one valley village to the hearing clinic, allowing ten minutes to walk together from the car to reception. He's anxious about getting the entrance wrong, so he clips the clinic's notice from the paper and recognises the new doorway when it appears on the local television news.

Fiona Singh works from her flat in the rail suburb between long drives to the branch offices where she trains new staff. She hears the headlines on television but bases her travel claims on the odometer, jotting down the reading before she gets out; an unclaimed return trip takes a noticeable bite out of her pay.

William Williams is retired and uses his big diesel to ferry folding tables between valley village halls, usually joining whichever collection run the volunteers arrange in their social group. He gets the sale dates from the paper and doesn't mind a change of plan, provided someone is at the door: there are only three minutes to unload before the bus needs its turning space.

Mohammed Nelson drives his diesel from a valley village to the bottling plant, picking up a workmate whose share of the mileage makes the long shifts worth the trip. He checks the television bulletin against the shift group's updates and usually takes the recommended route; missing their six-minute handover means the outgoing crew can't clock off together.

Oliver Morgan walks the children to school on the northern estate unless his mother has a morning clinic appointment; on those days he drives them all. A late start eats into the eight minutes he needs to get his mother from the car to reception, so a roadworks mention on the evening news is enough to make him ring the clinic about access.

Since retiring, Imran Fraser has collected unsold bread in his small diesel and taken it to lunch clubs across the valley villages. He spots requests in the village social group but lets the baker set the collection time: there's only a three-minute gap between the delivery vans at the back door.

Ruth Taylor does accounts from her kitchen in the market town and usually has clients send scans rather than driving out for their books. When a farmer has a whole box of receipts, she collects it on her longer Saturday trip to see her sister; after the television news she puts both addresses and the parking money in her bag.

Callum Nelson starts his home-care round on the northern estate and drives as far as the valley villages to help his last client into bed. A five-minute delay matters most at the house where two carers have to work together; whatever the staff chat says about traffic, he calls his partner there rather than changing the visit order himself.

Peter Hughes folds the seats down in his roomy petrol car to collect donated folding tables for the northern estate hall. The caretaker gives him three minutes at the loading door before the exercise class arrives, so Peter generally takes the approach the other retired volunteers recommend in their group chat, even if the television traffic map looks clear.

Jane Nelson drives her diesel the short distance from her market-town flat to open the bakery before the bread van arrives. She reads the road notices in yesterday's paper over breakfast; ten minutes early buys her time for a cup of tea with the night baker.

Nina Evans leaves the northern estate before dawn for a packaging shift well beyond the market town, taking a packed breakfast for the long drive. She pencils diversions from the local paper onto her route card and doesn't fret about a few extra miles if she gets her eight minutes in the canteen before clocking in.

Retired now, William Williams still drives boxes of large-print books from the southern estate library to readers scattered across the valley. He reads the paper, watches the news and follows the village group, but a disputed bridge closure keeps him worrying until he speaks to someone who's crossed it; the library has to pay him mileage for the long way round.

William Begum puts most of the miles on his diesel on the long drive from the valley villages to the office for design reviews. A television report about delays rarely settles the matter for him; if the rest of his team switches to video, he joins from home and saves a day's parking charge.

Sophie Lewis drives in from the outer ring to show new starters around the office, but she can do their paperwork with them by video. She trusts the travel bulletin on television more than the running commentary in the office chat and books parking by the half-day rather than paying to stay as long as everyone else.

Jane Green takes her granddaughter to breakfast club in her little diesel before collecting her father from his flat on the northern estate. He needs three minutes to get down in the lift, so she rings from the kerb and finishes the crossword in her paper while she waits.

Oliver Reed drives from the northern estate to collect his son and two other children whose parents cover the morning school run. He keeps the school's pick-up diagram from the local paper in the glovebox and passes official gate changes straight to the parents' group; six minutes in the wrong queue means missing the crossing patrol.

Jane Nelson drives a short loop through the rail suburb to take over the night desk at a residential home. She checks engineering notices in the paper because a delivery train can hold her at the crossing for eight minutes, and she hates making the day receptionist stay late.

Eleanor Allen leaves the rail suburb for distant client offices with a sample case that fits in the boot of her small petrol car. She checks the rail operator's own posts rather than polling colleagues: for a meeting that needs no samples, the train gives her a full hour to finish her figures.

Eleanor Walker keeps accounts from her outer-ring bungalow and uses her little diesel mainly to collect signed payroll sheets. She counts even five minutes of paid parking against the fee for a small payroll; if the television bulletin mentions delays, she asks the client to scan the sheets instead.

Harriet Jones drives the same three workmates from the outer ring to their early shift at the sorting shed, and their coins for petrol stay in the ashtray. They have an agreed three-minute wait at the last corner, and when the television bulletin gives a diversion she sticks to it so nobody has to guess where to stand.

Daniel Patel drives from the market town to a cold store where he has to sign for the first unloading shift in person. He checks the depot supervisor's posts over breakfast with the television on; ten minutes lost at the gate can leave a full trailer waiting for his signature.

Daniel Green carries three colleagues from the northern estate to a machine shop on the far side of the valley in his roomy petrol car. He checks the paper for road closures on Sundays and adds up the week's shared mileage then, so the apprentice on the back seat never has to find cash before payday.

Aisha Nelson makes a tight circuit of the southern estate in her diesel, helping one client dress before another client's breakfast call. She sees plenty of warnings in the carers' social group but rings the building caretaker about a blocked entrance; losing four minutes hunting for a side door cuts into the time she has to sit with someone.

Kiran Green's neighbour Kiran Walker drives a small petrol car between just a few streets in the rail suburb, carrying clean linen for morning care visits. Walker listens closely to the local television bulletin and worries more about losing five minutes at the level crossing than about the mileage: the first client's daughter can't leave for work until someone takes over.

William Green drives a large diesel between widely spaced home-care calls on the outer ring, with a folding shower chair strapped in the back. He gets route changes by phone from the coordinator and asks her to repeat the times; six minutes late for a two-person transfer leaves his partner waiting on the doorstep.

Harriet Davies can walk from her market-town flat to the office for most meetings and works at home the rest of the week, so her petrol car can stand untouched for weeks. She drives when it's her turn to bring the display boards, checking the team chat for the loading slot rather than assuming the five-minute bay is free.

Kiran Campbell drives a compact diesel from the northern estate to a specialist school across the valley, then takes a parent to physiotherapy on the return leg. Kiran keeps the times on a card supplied by the school secretary and allows ten minutes to get a walking frame out of the boot without rushing anyone.

Kiran Green uses a roomy diesel for a market-town school run that includes a niece, two sons and a cello. Kiran reads the paper's traffic column but asks the crossing guard which gate is actually open; four minutes saved at drop-off makes the difference between walking Grandad to the day centre and paying to park beside it.

Peter Lewis takes his diesel from a valley village to a distant office for contract signings, bundling several appointments into one day when clients agree. A closure notice in the weekly paper bothers him enough to call the highways desk for the exact hours: ten minutes is all he allows between the end of his drive and the first signature.

Rhys Allen can do most of his office work at the kitchen table on the outer ring, but on induction mornings he drives in to meet the new starter at reception. He listens to the local TV bulletin while he irons his shirt; the extra hour of parking costs enough that he tries not to arrive too early.

Jane Green is retired and drives her diesel from the northern estate to collect the lunch club's bread order on Wednesdays. She trusts the weather forecast on television and takes the earlier collection slot on wet mornings, when it takes longer to get the trays indoors under cover.

Sophie Kaur drives from the southern estate for a packing shift that starts before the first bus; her partner needs their petrol car back by two. She sees traffic reports on breakfast TV, but it's the photo of the depot gate in the shift group that tells her which entrance her colleagues are using.

Thomas Allen works from his northern-estate home between visits to two distant branch offices, where he has to sign off the stock counts in person. He trusts the travel times on the TV bulletin and books both counts for the same day when he can claim the whole diesel trip on one expenses form.

Leanne Green's early shift at the care home is only a short drive from the southern estate, but she has to stay for handover before she can take her little petrol car home. She watches the local TV news and does what the shift supervisor suggests about parking; another six minutes on foot leaves her sister waiting to use the car.

Thomas Morgan does accounts from his spare room on the northern estate and sometimes goes a week without moving his diesel car. The one appointment he keeps in person is his father's Friday hearing clinic; he watches the lunchtime news with his father afterwards, once the car is out of the paid bay.

Imran Lewis threads his small petrol car through the rail suburb on morning care rounds, with just three minutes between one client's breakfast call and the next client's door time. He reads the local paper and catches the TV news, but for access to a particular block he rings the caretaker who actually holds the gate key.

Kiran Owen drives out of the valley villages for office days with a visiting client and does the follow-up calls from home. Kiran asks the bus driver at the village stop about the return connection rather than following travel coverage; a ten-minute wait is fine, but a missed last bus means a costly taxi.

Peter Owen shares the drive from the outer ring with a colleague on the mornings they have to staff the office desk. He'll check a road notice from the TV news against the link in their neighbours' group, but he settles the departure time with his passenger: after nine, the cheap car park is usually full.

Rhys MacLeod drives from his valley village to minute the monthly board meeting; on ordinary office days he can join by phone. He listens closely to the TV travel bulletin and asks the chair to confirm the start time, since even a short delay at the single-lane bridge eats up his usual three minutes to set out the papers.

Mohammed Jones lives on the northern estate and covers two far-flung offices in his roomy petrol car, with days at home between trips. He follows the branches' official social accounts for opening notices and times the longer visit to avoid paying the evening rate at his daughter's after-school club.

Gareth MacLeod starts his care round in the rail suburb with a folding shower stool in the boot and a client who needs help getting up for breakfast. He allows ten minutes for the awkward parking behind the flats and treats tips in the carers' chat as leads, not directions, until someone on that street confirms them.

Fiona Morgan's market-town care round barely adds miles to her diesel, but she worries about the five minutes it can take to get from the square to a client's upstairs door. She watches the evening TV news, then calls the duty coordinator for the agreed access arrangements rather than guessing where she may park.

Rhys Evans leaves the northern estate for a long office commute when he has drawings to review in person; for a routine progress call he stays home. He reads the paper's road notices alongside posts from local drivers, but keeps his own log of journey times because ten minutes makes the difference between catching and missing school pickup.

Leanne Kaur's small diesel can sit outside her valley cottage for days while she works at home, but she has to open the office for the quarterly audit. Anxious about keeping the auditors waiting, she checks the dates on diversions in the weekly paper and the village group rather than taking a neighbour's usual shortcut on trust.

Daniel Iqbal drives from the market town for the late bakery shift, when the mixers have to be running before the dough crew arrives. He catches the TV news and reads the bakery's posts without getting rattled; if a colleague is covering the last batch, he can share a lift home and split the parking charge.

Bethan Campbell drives out of the rail suburb to oversee file transfers at a distant office, though on days without boxes she can work from home or take the train. She clips engineering notices from the paper and listens for changes on TV, worried that a missed connection will leave her paying for another hour of childcare.

Ruth Evans takes the children from the outer ring to school in the family diesel, then picks up her mother for physiotherapy. She gets the appointment time from the receptionist and the gate time from the school secretary; there's only a four-minute cushion if her mother needs the walker brought round to the passenger door.

William MacLeod can take the train from the rail suburb for most office meetings, but drives when it's his turn to bring the display stands. A five-minute overrun at the station costs him the express, so he compares the timetable in the paper with TV updates and the operator's social feed rather than relying on the chatter on the platform.

Imran Williams takes his small diesel from the northern estate to unlock the workshop before the six o'clock shift. He notices road announcements on TV, in the paper and on the council's social feed, but measures both routes himself; the crew's favourite shortcut costs him six minutes at a locked yard gate.

Oliver MacLeod drives from the northern estate to a loading bay on the far side of town, where a late start means losing his pick of the paid overtime slots. He watches the evening bulletin and reads the shift chat, but sets his alarm by the gate time on his own rota, not by when the others say they're leaving.

Jaspreet Evans takes a diesel from the rail suburb to the laundry's first shift because the passenger trains don't stop near the service entrance. Jaspreet trusts the local TV travel notices and sticks to the posted diversion; there's barely time to change shoes in the three minutes between clocking in and the first trolley.

William Jones has a long drive from the northern estate to relieve the operator at a pumping station, who cannot leave the controls unattended. Even after checking the TV forecast and the road column in the paper, he frets about making his colleague stay late and follows the supervisor's advice to leave before the school traffic.

Mohammed Campbell drives his son to school in the rail suburb and then takes his aunt shopping while the supermarket is quiet enough for her to use her walking frame. He watches local TV and reads the paper, but follows the school's own posts for gate changes: ten minutes spent circling the wrong entrance comes straight out of his aunt's shopping time.

Leanne Reed lives close enough to her office on the southern estate to walk in for most meetings, using her petrol car only when the archive cartons have to go back. She catches the local news on TV but phones reception for the loading slot; with the trolley waiting at the door, she can unload in three minutes without buying a parking ticket.

Fiona Iqbal does accounts from her flat in the rail suburb and walks to the station for her monthly client visit unless she has a box of ledgers to carry. She checks the timetable beside the ticket machine herself; the slower train still gets her there on time and costs less than parking.

Since retiring, Oliver Iqbal has collected donated bread from the market town's baker on Tuesdays, just before the shutters come down. He checks the volunteer group's messages over the evening television news and takes the handcart if there are only a couple of trays.

Leanne Singh drives her little diesel between two valley villages, dropping the children at school before helping her mother get washed and dressed. She reads road notices in the local paper and checks the school's own messages rather than taking another parent's shortcut; her mother's breakfast is already late if the run slips ten minutes.

Bethan Jones makes short home-care calls around the rail suburb, with eight minutes between helping one client into his coat and meeting another at her bath seat. She reads the notices in the paper, but for the awkward turn under the railway she takes the route the early carers recommend in their group chat.

Leanne Campbell drives a roomy diesel around the outer ring, where her first client needs help getting up before the day-centre minibus arrives. With the television on over breakfast, she checks which entrance the night carer used at the flats; following her in saves eight minutes of walking round the block.

Leanne Taylor drives out of the market town for the first packing shift because the early bus arrives six minutes after clock-in. A closing date for the bridge in the local paper doesn't match the one she heard on television, so she rings the depot before setting her alarm; she can't afford to lose the attendance bonus.

On office days Jaspreet Owen drives from the outer ring to present drawings that are too large to spread out at home. A vague traffic item on breakfast television leaves her watching the clock, so she checks the team chat and usually shares a lift with whichever colleague has a parking space booked.

Thomas Allen drives his diesel between home-care visits in the rail suburb, including a ten-minute crossing to help a man transfer from bed to chair with a second carer. He takes changes directly from the coordinator by phone and repeats the time back, because his partner on the lift cannot start alone.

Leanne Nelson lives in the rail suburb only a short drive from the laundry where she works, but the walk home after the late shift takes forty minutes. She worries about paying for a taxi and asks the supervisor to confirm the finish time rather than counting on a lift mentioned in the shift chat.

Eleanor Reed drives from the market town to relieve the night porter, leaving ten minutes to count the keys together. She folds the paper's street-closure map into her work bag and checks the dates on the signs herself; a lively argument in the town group doesn't usually change her route.

Imran Morgan keeps accounts from his outer-ring home, but his fortnightly trip to see his father and stock his freezer puts plenty of miles on the petrol car. He uses the family chat to find out who's already going and splits the grocery list with his sister so neither pays for a second long drive.

Fiona Campbell does accounts at home on the southern estate and makes frequent short trips in her small petrol car to collect receipt envelopes from shopkeepers. She circles their half-day closing times in the paper and follows the other bookkeeper's collection order so she is back at her desk for the afternoon payroll.

Nina Morgan is retired and drives a small diesel from the northern estate to take people to outpatient appointments, sometimes making the long trip twice in a day. Conflicting road reports in the paper and on television bother her, so she phones the volunteer who did yesterday's run and leaves the same extra quarter hour.

William Morgan does accounts at home on the northern estate and drives his little petrol car across town when a client needs original invoices collected. He'll read a parking tip in the traders' group, but he still checks the tariff on the meter: an hour's parking comes straight out of his collection fee.

Alison Morgan's school run starts on the southern estate and ends several miles beyond the school at her father's house, where she helps him with breakfast. She goes by the school's printed gate times rather than other parents' estimates and lays out his porridge things the night before to save five minutes.

Callum Lewis drives in from the outer ring for hands-on training sessions and does his desk work at home. He checks the office chat before booking a desk and generally picks the same day as his teammate, who shares the parking charge and knows which entrance opens early.

Peter Singh drives his children from the southern estate to school and takes his aunt to her exercise class on the return leg. He uses the parents' group for reminders but keeps the class card clipped to his visor; five minutes spent at the wrong gate would eat into the half hour his aunt has paid for.

Daniel Begum is retired and uses his small diesel to take a folding display and a tin of change to the rail suburb's weekly repair café. He ignores most online chatter but copies the setup crew's arrival time from their group chat, since the ten-minute loading space is free only while he's unloading.

Eleanor Campbell works on accounts at home on the northern estate, though she regularly drives a long way to rehearse with a choir. She worries about the cost of making the trip alone and checks the singers' chat before leaving, usually joining the car share the other altos have arranged.

Ruth Shah drives in from the outer ring to start the ovens at a wholesale bakery before the first bus runs. She picks up the mixer operator at the junction he posts in the shift chat; it adds four minutes, and he pays for his share of the petrol on payday.

Jaspreet MacLeod keeps accounts from the southern estate but drives a small diesel across the valley for weekend hockey. The players agree on lifts in their group chat, and Jaspreet usually takes the kit bags when someone else collects the goalkeeper, sparing both drivers a long detour.

Fiona Davies works at home between long drives from the northern estate to the office for staff inductions. She listens to the breakfast television travel report and sets off with the other trainer when their schedules match, so they only pay for one all-day parking ticket.

Callum Green starts his home-care round on the northern estate, with six minutes to get from a client's breakfast call to a bungalow where two carers are needed for a lift.
